planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained, acidic soil; in marginal zone 9b gardens grow Peerless in a large container that can be sheltered, or in the warmest protected microclimate available, since lychee wood is damaged by hard freezes.

directions: Peerless is a historic Florida lychee cultivar that originated at the Royal Palm Nursery and was documented as a heavy, reliable bearer with larger, brighter-colored fruit than the industry-standard Brewster. A high percentage of its seeds are abortive (small or undeveloped), meaning more of each fruit is edible aril, which made it popular with Florida growers in the early-to-mid twentieth century. Like other lychee cultivars, Peerless has essentially no frost tolerance and needs acidic, well-drained soil and a wind-protected, south-facing site; in zone 9b, container culture with winter shelter is the most reliable approach. Mulch the root zone heavily each winter, since lychee roots are sensitive to cold and to waterlogged soil.
sources: Morton, J. 1987. Fruits of Warm Climates - Lychee
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Lychee Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained, acidic soil; site it in the warmest, most sheltered part of the garden or grow it in a large movable container, since lychee has no meaningful frost tolerance.

directions: Late Globe is a historic Florida lychee selection, a seedling chosen by Col. Grove and believed by Professor Groff to be a natural hybrid of Brewster and the Mountain lychee type, chosen for its distinctly late ripening window compared to most other cultivars. That later harvest timing can extend the usable lychee season for a dooryard planting and spreads out the workload of a small home orchard. As with all lychee, Late Globe demands acidic, well-drained soil, consistent moisture during fruit development, and full protection from frost and hard freezes; in zone 9b it should be grown as a container specimen or sited against a south-facing wall with heavy winter mulching over the root zone.
sources: Morton, J. 1987. Fruits of Warm Climates - Lychee

common_name: Pat Po Heung Lychee (Hawaiian Heirloom Lychee)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained, acidic soil; the slow, weak, spreading growth habit of Pat Po Heung makes it a reasonable candidate for a large container in marginal zones, where it can be moved to shelter during cold snaps.

directions: Pat Po Heung is an older Hawaiian lychee cultivar noted for a slow, weak, spreading growth habit that nonetheless bears well and produces dependable fruit set once the tree is established. Its lower, wider-spreading stature can be an advantage in home gardens with limited vertical space or in large containers at the cooler margin of lychee range. It shares the same cultural needs as other lychee cultivars: acidic, well-drained soil, steady moisture through fruit development, and complete protection from frost, since lychee wood and roots are both damaged by freezing temperatures. In zone 9b, overwinter container specimens in a greenhouse or garage near a bright window, or site in-ground trees against a heat-retaining south wall with deep winter mulch.
sources: Morton, J. 1987. Fruits of Warm Climates - Lychee
